results.title: How to Deal With Regret: The Ultimate Guide to Move on From Regret
results.content: ## What is Regret? ## The Science Behind Regret. Thomas Gilovich, the leading researcher on regret, conducted a groundbreaking study called “The Experience of Regret: What, When, Why.” His findings revealed something fascinating: **while most of us experience regret, it doesn’t naturally fade over time without active processing.** This discovery changed how psychologists understand the long-term impact of our choices. * **54% regretted actions not taken**. * 12% regretted actions they took. ### Educational Regrets. ### Career Regrets. These regrets tend to intensify around mid-career, when people have enough experience to recognize missed opportunities but may feel it’s too late to make major changes. ### Relationship Regrets. ## Why We Experience Regret. Regret serves an important evolutionary purpose—think of it as your brain’s built-in learning system, carefully designed to help you make better choices and avoid repeating mistakes. In fact, research shows that children who experience more regret tend to make better decisions and show greater delayed gratification. When we experience regret, our brains engage in a sophisticated process that shapes our future behavior. ## How to Deal with Regret. Also, talk about this regret. One of the most effective ways to prevent future regrets is adopting what I like to call an “experimental mindset.” Think of your life as a laboratory where each experience provides valuable data for your personal growth. * What experiences would I regret not trying? The internal work of processing regret is just as important as external actions. **Can regret be good for you?**. Studies indicate that people who experience and process regret effectively make better decisions in the future and show increased personal growth. To minimize future regrets, make decisions based on your values rather than others’ expectations. Research shows that up to 82% of people experience regret about major life choices at some point. When people consider how they might regret their choices in the future, they tend to make more thoughtful, value-aligned decisions in the present. By understanding your regrets, processing them healthily, and taking action to address them, you can transform these painful experiences into powerful tools for personal growth.Ready to take the next step in your emotional healing journey?

results.title: How to Cope With Regret
results.content: * Accepting your feelings and forgiving yourself can help you move past regret. * Use regrets as learning opportunities to make better choices in the future. Life is full of choices and paths not taken, so it isn’t surprising that people sometimes feel regret over both the decisions they made and the ones they didn’t. The problem is that when you are feeling regret over past choices or past mistakes, you might sometimes miss out on the joys of the present moment. The reason why regret feels so awful is because, by its nature, it implies that there is something you could have done, some choice you could have made, or some action you might have taken that would have made something good happen or avoided something terrible. Regret is a difficult thing to feel, but some experts suggest it can also have a positive impact if you cope with it well and allow it to help you make better choices going forward. Or take the negativity out of these feelings and turn your regrets into opportunities for growth and change. Efforts to avoid future regrets can help you make better decisions.3. Because regret involves a component of guilt and self-recrimination, finding ways to forgive yourself can help relieve some of the negative feelings associated with regret. One way to help cope with feelings of regret is to use those experiences to fuel future action. Changing how you think about things that have happened in the past can also help you see regret in a different way. ### Regret. In addition to regretting choices, people often regret not taking certain actions in the past. And when people think that not taking action will lead to feelings of regret (such as not taking care of their health or not engaging in regular exercise), they become more likely to take steps to avoid those anticipated regrets.8. Studies have also found that concern about anticipated regret can influence the decisions that people make on the behalf of others.9 When people are worried that people are going to be disappointed or regretful, they are more likely to make more conservative choices.

results.title: How to Deal with Guilt or Regret
results.content: I’d love to offer a few practices that may help you on your way, but first I’d like to say: I’m sorry you’re on the trail, at all, my friend. And I’m sorry for whatever circumstances added guilt to the grief you already feel. # 3 Practices to Help You Process Guilt or Regret. Whenever we’re wracked with guilt or regret, we’re trying to live inside the unchangeable past. That’s especially true when we feel regret over our interactions (or lack thereof) with a loved one who’s passed on. The mere suggestion of that party melted my brain and made me shout, “I’m not ready for that!” He never got to have that gathering and, to this day, I still wish I’d handled that moment differently. * I’m disappointed that I wasn’t my best self in that moment. Our next healing practice can be best expressed in the immortal words of Charles Wright: “Express yourself.” (“Jumpin’ like a kangaroo” optional. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve replayed the phrase: “I’m not ready for that!” in my head. If you feel the same, find a private moment and have a conversation with your loved one either out loud or in your heart. * **Find a flashlight:** Navigating grief is tough, especially when it’s laced with guilt or regret. It’s normal to feel regret, remorse or even guilt after a loved one “gets on the bus.” The antidote is grace every time. When I’m being too hard on myself, I find it helpful to look at a picture of me when I was little. When I am filled with regret, I have to say to myself, I was there for her, did the best I could for her, and loved her. You don’t know how things would have turned out if you made different decisions – things may have been worse than they are now.” So why can’t I say that to myself? I feel like I messed up their lives, even though I know I didn’t.
